```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.align = "center")
source("R/00_config.R")
library(knitr); library(leaflet)
crash <- readRDS(out_path("crash_clustered.rds"))
val   <- readRDS(out_path("validation.rds"))
dca   <- readRDS(out_path("dca_comparison.rds"))
prof  <- readRDS(out_path("profiles.rds"))
P <- prof$profiles; S <- prof$stories
pct <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
num <- function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ",")
k <- val$k

years <- as.numeric(diff(range(crash$date)) + 1) / 365.25
total_deaths  <- sum(crash$n_killed)
total_serious <- sum(crash$n_serious)
P <- P |> mutate(deaths_per_1000 = 1000 * deaths / n, deaths_per_year = deaths / years,
                 serious_per_year = serious / years, cl = as.character(cluster))

# Labels, colours and helpers shared by every table and figure.
cols  <- situation_colours(k)
lab   <- setNames(sprintf("%s. %s", P$cl, P$name), P$cl)
short <- setNames(tolower(sub(",[^,]*$", "", P$name)), P$cl)       # first two traits
swatch <- function(cl) sprintf('<span class="sw" style="background:%s"></span>%s', cols[cl], lab[cl])
to_situation <- function(x) gsub("\\bcluster\\b", "situation", gsub("\\bCluster\\b", "Situation", x))
tbl <- function(df, ...) kable(df, format = "html", escape = FALSE, row.names = FALSE,
                               table.attr = 'class="table rtable"', ...)
theme_report <- function(base = 12) theme_minimal(base_size = base) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = base + 2), plot.title.position = "plot",
        plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey35"), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), axis.text = element_text(colour = "grey25"))

# Clusters referred to in the text, found by rule so the text follows the data.
find_cl <- function(pattern) P$cl[grepl(pattern, P$name)][1]
c_rural <- P$cl[which.max(P$rural)]
c_night <- find_cl("night")
c_ped   <- P$cl[which.max(P$top_dca_group == "Pedestrian" & P$top_dca_share > 0.5)]
c_bike  <- find_cl("Cyclist")
c_rain  <- find_cl("Rain")
c_poor  <- find_cl("Poorly recorded")
c_big   <- P$cl[which.max(P$n)]
top2    <- P$cl[order(-P$deaths)][1:2]
pr <- function(cl) P[P$cl == cl, ]

# The official category hiding the widest range of death rates across situations
# (situations with 500+ crashes in that category; the poorly recorded cluster excluded).
dca_split <- crash |>
  filter(as.character(cluster) != c_poor) |>
  group_by(dca_group, cluster) |>
  summarise(n = n(), deaths = sum(n_killed), fatal_rate = mean(fatal), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(n >= 500) |>
  mutate(deaths_per_1000 = 1000 * deaths / n)
split_rank <- dca_split |> group_by(dca_group) |>
  summarise(ratio = max(deaths_per_1000) / min(deaths_per_1000)) |> arrange(-ratio)
ex_group <- as.character(split_rank$dca_group[1])
ex <- dca_split |> filter(dca_group == ex_group) |> arrange(-deaths_per_1000)
ex_hi <- ex[1, ]; ex_lo <- ex[nrow(ex), ]
fold  <- round(ex_hi$deaths_per_1000 / ex_lo$deaths_per_1000)

ag <- dca$agree; sm <- dca$sev_models
auc_dca  <- sm$AUC[sm$outcome == "fatal" & sm$model == "DCA group only"]
auc_both <- sm$AUC[sm$outcome == "fatal" & sm$model == "DCA group + cluster"]
top2_deaths <- sum(P$share_of_deaths[P$cl %in% top2])
top2_share  <- sum(P$share[P$cl %in% top2])
```

# Summary {-}

<div class="stats">
<div class="stat"><div class="num">`r num(total_deaths)`</div><div class="lbl">people killed in Victorian road crashes, `r format(min(crash$date), "%Y")`–`r format(max(crash$date), "%Y")`</div></div>
<div class="stat"><div class="num">`r round(total_deaths / years)`</div><div class="lbl">deaths every year, and `r num(total_serious / years)` serious injuries</div></div>
<div class="stat accent"><div class="num">`r pct(top2_deaths)`</div><div class="lbl">of deaths come from just two situations, which make up only `r pct(top2_share)` of crashes</div></div>
<div class="stat accent"><div class="num">`r fold`×</div><div class="lbl">difference in death rate hidden inside a single official crash category</div></div>
</div>

::: {.callout}
**Question.** If Victoria could make one kind of road situation safer, which would save the most lives?

**Answer.** Grouping `r num(nrow(crash))` police-reported crashes by the *situation* they happened in, rather than the
official crash category, shows that deaths are heavily concentrated in two situations:

* **High-speed roads, mostly rural, often a single vehicle:** `r pct(pr(c_rural)$share)` of crashes but
  **`r num(pr(c_rural)$deaths)` deaths (`r pct(pr(c_rural)$share_of_deaths)`)**, about `r round(pr(c_rural)$deaths_per_year)` a year.
* **Night-time, often young drivers:** `r pct(pr(c_night)$share)` of crashes but
  **`r num(pr(c_night)$deaths)` deaths (`r pct(pr(c_night)$share_of_deaths)`)**.

The **most common** situation, city intersections (`r pct(pr(c_big)$share)` of crashes), is **not** the most deadly.
A high-speed rural crash is `r sprintf("%.1f", pr(c_rural)$deaths_per_1000 / pr(c_big)$deaths_per_1000)` times as
likely to kill someone.
:::

::: {.callout .key}
**Why it matters.** Victoria's official crash categories (DCA codes) record *how* a crash happened, such as "head-on"
or "ran off the road", but not the situation. Within the single category "`r ex_group`", crashes in one situation
killed **`r round(ex_hi$deaths_per_1000)` people per 1,000 crashes** and in another only
**`r sprintf("%.1f", ex_lo$deaths_per_1000)`**. Counting crashes by category points attention at where crashes are
*common*; counting deaths by situation points it at where people *die*.

**What should be done** (Section 6): make high-speed rural roads and night-time driving the two priority situations,
keep protecting pedestrians in the inner city, and improve how police record crash conditions.
:::

# Why this question matters

Road-safety resources are limited, so every dollar spent on one location or campaign is a dollar not spent elsewhere.
Agencies usually report crashes using the police **Definition for Classifying Accidents (DCA)**, which describes the
movement of the vehicles and people involved (rear-end, right-turn, pedestrian struck, off road on a curve...).

That tells you *how* a crash happened but not *what situation the driver was in*: the road, speed limit, time, light,
weather, and who was involved. Two crashes with the same DCA code can be completely different events. One is a 50 km/h
side-swipe in a city street; the other is a 110 km/h head-on on a dark rural highway.

We asked four questions:

1. What crash **situations** emerge if we let the data group crashes by their conditions?
2. **Which situations cost the most lives**, and where in Victoria do they happen?
3. Do these situations repeat the official categories, or **reveal risk the categories miss**?
4. What does that mean for **where road-safety effort should go**?

# The answer: lives lost in each situation

We grouped all `r num(nrow(crash))` crashes into `r k` situations using 17 descriptions of the conditions (Section 7
explains how). The grouping didn't use the outcome, the official category or the location. Those were kept aside so we
could test the situations against them.

```{r lives-chart, fig.width=10.5, fig.height=5}
ord <- P$cl[order(P$share_of_deaths)]
lives <- P |>
  select(cl, share, share_of_deaths) |>
  pivot_longer(-cl, names_to = "measure", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(measure = factor(measure, c("share_of_deaths", "share"), c("Share of deaths", "Share of crashes")),
         cl = factor(cl, levels = ord))
ggplot(lives, aes(value, cl, fill = measure)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.78), width = 0.72) +
  geom_text(aes(label = pct(value)), position = position_dodge(width = 0.78), hjust = -0.15, size = 3.4,
            colour = "grey20") +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = function(x) str_wrap(lab[x], 42)) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, expand = expansion(c(0, 0.1))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Share of crashes" = "#b8c4d1", "Share of deaths" = "#D1495B"),
                    breaks = c("Share of crashes", "Share of deaths")) +
  labs(title = "Some situations kill far more people than their crash numbers suggest",
       subtitle = sprintf("%s people killed, %s to %s", num(total_deaths), format(min(crash$date), "%Y"),
                          format(max(crash$date), "%Y")),
       x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_report() + theme(legend.position = "top", legend.justification = "left")
```

```{r lives-table}
tbl(P |> arrange(-deaths) |>
      transmute(Situation = swatch(cl), Crashes = num(n), `People killed` = num(deaths),
                `Killed per year` = round(deaths_per_year), `Seriously injured per year` = num(serious_per_year),
                `Deaths per 1,000 crashes` = sprintf("%.1f", deaths_per_1000),
                `Share of all deaths` = pct(share_of_deaths)),
    align = "lrrrrrr")
```

Three things stand out:

* **Danger is not where crashes are most common.** City intersection crashes (situation `r c_big`) are the most
  frequent, but they kill `r sprintf("%.1f", pr(c_big)$deaths_per_1000)` people per 1,000 crashes. High-speed rural
  crashes kill `r sprintf("%.1f", pr(c_rural)$deaths_per_1000)`, night-time crashes
  `r sprintf("%.1f", pr(c_night)$deaths_per_1000)`, and pedestrian crashes `r sprintf("%.1f", pr(c_ped)$deaths_per_1000)`.
* **Speed and darkness are the common thread** in the two deadliest situations. Both are cases where a mistake is
  harder to survive or harder to see coming.
* **Cyclist crashes are frequent but rarely fatal.** Situation `r c_bike` holds `r pct(pr(c_bike)$share)` of crashes
  but `r pct(pr(c_bike)$share_of_deaths)` of deaths. These crashes still cause
  `r num(pr(c_bike)$serious_per_year)` serious injuries a year.

```{r severity-fig, out.width="100%"}
include_graphics(fig_path("severity_by_cluster.png"))
```

# What the official categories miss

## The same official category, a different chance of dying

```{r dca-example}
tbl(ex |> transmute(Situation = swatch(as.character(cluster)), Crashes = num(n), `People killed` = deaths,
                    `Deaths per 1,000 crashes` = sprintf("%.1f", deaths_per_1000),
                    `Crashes that killed someone` = pct(fatal_rate, 1)),
    align = "lrrrr",
    caption = sprintf("Every crash in this table has the same official category: \"%s\".", ex_group))
```

::: {.callout .key}
Every crash above has the same official label, "`r ex_group`". In the **`r short[as.character(ex_hi$cluster)]`**
situation, **`r pct(ex_hi$fatal_rate, 1)` of them killed someone**. In the **`r short[as.character(ex_lo$cluster)]`**
situation, `r pct(ex_lo$fatal_rate, 1)` did. A report that only counts crashes by category treats these as one
problem. They are very different problems that need different solutions.
:::

## Situations and categories only partly overlap

```{r heatmap, out.width="100%"}
include_graphics(fig_path("dca_heatmap.png"))
```

The agreement between our situations and the official categories is low (adjusted Rand index
`r sprintf("%.2f", ag$ARI[1])`, where 0 means no agreement and 1 means identical). The one clear exception is
**pedestrians**: `r pct(pr(c_ped)$top_dca_share)` of situation `r c_ped` is the official "Pedestrian" category. When a
pedestrian is involved, who was hit defines both groupings. Everywhere else, situations such as rain or darkness cut
across every kind of crash movement.

## Knowing the situation improves the prediction of deaths

We tested whether the situation tells us anything about the outcome *beyond* the official category, using logistic
regression to predict whether a crash was fatal.

```{r sev-models}
tbl(sm |> filter(outcome == "fatal") |>
      transmute(`Predicting a fatal crash using...` = to_situation(model),
                `AUC (0.5 = guessing, 1 = perfect)` = sprintf("%.3f", AUC),
                `Improvement test (p-value)` = ifelse(is.na(lrt_p_cluster_added), "",
                                                      format.pval(lrt_p_cluster_added, digits = 2))),
    align = "lrr")
```

Adding the situation to the official category improves the prediction of fatal crashes
(AUC `r sprintf("%.2f", auc_dca)` → `r sprintf("%.2f", auc_both)`), and the improvement is far beyond chance
(likelihood-ratio test). **The situation carries life-or-death information that the official category doesn't
record.** The prediction is still far from perfect, because the data doesn't include impact speed, seatbelt use or
traffic volumes.

# The seven situations, told as stories

Each situation is described three ways: its **profile** (calculated from all its crashes), a **typical crash** (the
most common value of each condition, combined into one picture) and a **real crash from the data** whose details are
most typical of the situation. They're ordered from most deaths to fewest.

```{r stories, results="asis"}
for (j in order(-P$deaths)) {
  cl <- P$cl[j]
  hot <- P$deaths_per_1000[j] > 1000 * total_deaths / nrow(crash)
  cat(sprintf("\n\n## Situation %s: %s\n\n", cl, P$name[j]))
  cat(sprintf('<div class="card" style="--c:%s">\n<div class="meta">', cols[cl]))
  cat(sprintf('<span class="pill%s">%s people killed (%s of all deaths)</span>', if (hot) " hot" else "",
              num(P$deaths[j]), pct(P$share_of_deaths[j])))
  cat(sprintf('<span class="pill%s">%.1f deaths per 1,000 crashes</span>', if (hot) " hot" else "", P$deaths_per_1000[j]))
  cat(sprintf('<span class="pill">%s crashes (%s)</span><span class="pill">%s</span></div>\n',
              num(P$n[j]), pct(P$share[j], 1), P$where[j]))
  cat(sprintf('<div class="story"><b>Typical crash.</b> %s</div>\n', S$typical_story[j]))
  cat(sprintf('<div class="story"><b>%s.</b> %s</div>\n', sub("\\):.*", ")", S$real_story[j]),
              sub("^[^:]*: ", "", S$real_story[j])))
  cat(sprintf('<p class="profile">%s</p>\n</div>\n', to_situation(S$description[j])))
}
```

## Interactive map

Use the boxes in the top-right corner to turn situations on and off. Every fatal crash is shown, larger and outlined,
together with 8,000 randomly chosen other crashes. Click a point for details. The Shiny app (`shiny::runApp("app")`)
has the full version with year, severity and region filters and story cards.

```{r leaflet}
set.seed(SEED)
m <- crash |> filter(!is.na(lat)) |>
  (\(d) bind_rows(d |> filter(!fatal) |> slice_sample(n = 8000), d |> filter(fatal)))() |>
  mutate(cl = as.character(cluster))
grp <- setNames(sprintf('<span class="sw" style="background:%s"></span>%s', cols[P$cl], lab[P$cl]), P$cl)
map <- leaflet(width = "100%", height = 560, options = leafletOptions(preferCanvas = TRUE)) |>
  addProviderTiles(BASEMAP) |>
  addTiles(urlTemplate = BASEMAP_LABELS, options = tileOptions(pane = "overlayPane")) |>
  fitBounds(141, -39.2, 150, -34)
for (cl in P$cl) {
  d <- m[m$cl == cl, ]
  map <- map |>
    addCircleMarkers(data = d, lng = ~lon, lat = ~lat, group = grp[[cl]],
                     radius = ~ifelse(fatal, 4, 2.5), stroke = ~fatal, color = "#ffffff", weight = 0.8,
                     fillColor = cols[[cl]], fillOpacity = ~ifelse(fatal, 0.95, 0.6),
                     popup = ~sprintf("<b>%s</b><br>%s, %s<br>%s, %s<br>%s<br><b>%s</b>",
                                      lab[cl], format(date, "%d %b %Y"), time, lga, region, dca_desc, severity))
}
map |> addLayersControl(overlayGroups = unname(grp), options = layersControlOptions(collapsed = FALSE))
```

# Recommendations

These recommendations follow from the evidence above. The *measures* are well-established road-safety approaches; our
analysis shows **where** they would address the most harm, not how well each one works. That would need evaluation
data we don't have.

```{r recs, results="asis"}
recs <- list(
  list(cl = c_rural, title = "Make high-speed rural roads more forgiving",
       ev = sprintf("%s deaths (%s of all), about %d a year · %.1f deaths per 1,000 crashes · %s of these crashes are rural · most over-represented in %s",
                    num(pr(c_rural)$deaths), pct(pr(c_rural)$share_of_deaths), round(pr(c_rural)$deaths_per_year),
                    pr(c_rural)$deaths_per_1000, pct(pr(c_rural)$rural), pr(c_rural)$overrep_lgas),
       do = "Protective infrastructure (barriers, rumble strips, sealed shoulders) and speed management on high-speed roads where single-vehicle crashes cluster.",
       who = c("Department of Transport and Planning")),
  list(cl = c_night, title = "Target night-time driving, especially by young drivers",
       ev = sprintf("%s deaths (%s of all) · %.1f deaths per 1,000 crashes · a driver or rider aged 16-25 involved in nearly half",
                    num(pr(c_night)$deaths), pct(pr(c_night)$share_of_deaths), pr(c_night)$deaths_per_1000),
       do = "Night-time conditions in graduated licensing, better lighting at night-time crash locations, and enforcement focused on evening and late-night hours.",
       who = c("Licensing authority", "Road-safety campaigns", "Victoria Police")),
  list(cl = c_ped, title = "Keep protecting pedestrians in the inner city",
       ev = sprintf("%s deaths · %.1f deaths per 1,000 crashes · concentrated in %s",
                    num(pr(c_ped)$deaths), pr(c_ped)$deaths_per_1000, pr(c_ped)$overrep_lgas),
       do = "Lower speeds and safer crossings where pedestrians and traffic mix.",
       who = c("Local councils", "Department of Transport and Planning")),
  list(cl = c_rain, title = "Treat the roads where rain turns deadly",
       ev = sprintf("%s deaths · %.1f deaths per 1,000 crashes · over-represented in %s",
                    num(pr(c_rain)$deaths), pr(c_rain)$deaths_per_1000, pr(c_rain)$overrep_lgas),
       do = "Skid-resistant surfacing and wet-weather warnings on the most affected roads.",
       who = c("Department of Transport and Planning", "Local councils")),
  list(cl = c_poor, title = "Record every crash fully",
       ev = sprintf("%s of crashes have weather, surface or speed zone missing · they are the least severe, so minor crashes are documented least",
                    pct(pr(c_poor)$share)),
       do = "Make weather, surface and speed zone mandatory in police crash reports, so future analysis isn't biased toward serious crashes.",
       who = c("Victoria Police"))
)
for (i in seq_along(recs)) {
  r <- recs[[i]]
  cat(sprintf(paste0('<div class="rec" style="--c:%s"><div class="n">%d</div><div>',
                     '<h4>%s</h4><div class="ev">%s</div><div class="do">%s</div>',
                     '<div class="who">Who could act: %s</div></div></div>\n'),
              cols[[r$cl]], i, r$title, r$ev, r$do,
              paste(sprintf("<span>%s</span>", r$who), collapse = " ")))
}
```

::: {.callout}
**The scale of the prize.** Every **10% reduction in deaths in the high-speed rural situation alone would mean about
`r round(0.1 * pr(c_rural)$deaths_per_year)` fewer people killed each year**. That is simple arithmetic on the averages
above, not a forecast.
:::

# How we did it

## Data

The Victorian Crash Data release has nine linked tables. We joined them in R (`R/01_prepare.R`) into one row per crash:
the accident record, the location, the most adverse weather and road surface, flags for the vehicles involved
(motorcycle, bicycle, heavy vehicle, the oldest vehicle's age, the strictest traffic control) and flags for the people
involved (pedestrian, driver or rider aged 16-25 or 70+). The raw data is 168 MB and runs in R on a laptop in a few
minutes; Hadoop was not needed. Missing values were kept as "Unknown" rather than dropped. That decision revealed the
poorly-recorded situation.

## Grouping crashes into situations

```{r features}
tbl(data.frame(
  Condition = FEATURE_LABELS[CLUSTER_FEATURES],
  Categories = sapply(CLUSTER_FEATURES, function(f) paste(sprintf("%s (%s)", levels(crash[[f]]),
                      pct(prop.table(table(crash[[f]])))), collapse = ", "))))
```

Because the conditions are categories, not numbers, we used **Multiple Correspondence Analysis (MCA)**, the
categorical version of PCA, to turn them into `r val$n_dims` numeric dimensions. We then grouped the crashes with
**k-means**. The official category, accident type, severity and location were deliberately left out, so the
comparisons in Sections 3 and 4 are fair tests rather than circular ones.

We tested 4 to 14 groups and chose `r k`. To be chosen, a solution had to come back almost identically from different
random starts and from different halves of the data. Among the stable solutions, `r k` gave the best-separated groups
while still separating pedestrian, cyclist, night-time and wet-weather crashes. We also prototyped **Gower distance +
PAM**, but its groups changed from sample to sample, so we only used it as a cross-check.

```{r validation}
tbl(data.frame(
  Check = c("Same groups from different random starts (ARI, 1 = identical)",
            "Same groups from different halves of the data (ARI)",
            "Separation between groups (silhouette, -1 to 1)"),
  Result = c(sprintf("%.2f", val$seed_stability), sprintf("%.2f", val$subsample_stability),
             sprintf("%.2f", val$silhouette))), align = "lr")
```

The groups are very **stable** but not sharply **separated**. Crashes don't fall into perfectly distinct types,
because most share common conditions (daylight, dry road, weekday). The situations are best read as reliable regions
of a continuum, so we interpret their overall profiles, not individual crash assignments.

## Comparing with the official categories

We compared situations with DCA groups using cross-tables, the adjusted Rand index and normalised mutual information,
and tested whether the situation adds predictive information about fatal crashes using logistic regression and a
likelihood-ratio test (`R/03_compare_dca.R`). The stories in Section 4 are generated in R from each situation's
statistics and from a real crash record (`R/04_profile_stories.R`).

# Limitations

* **No traffic volumes.** We know where people died, not how many trips were made. A situation with many deaths may
  partly reflect a lot of driving. Deaths *per crash* (used throughout) is not affected by this.
* **Recommendations show where, not what works.** The analysis identifies where harm is concentrated. Choosing between
  measures needs evaluation studies.
* **Situations depend on the conditions we chose.** A different set of conditions would give somewhat different
  groups. We explain every exclusion above.
* **Groups overlap.** They are stable but not sharply separated (silhouette `r sprintf("%.2f", val$silhouette)`).
* **Injury crashes only.** Crashes with only property damage aren't in the data.
* **Recording gaps.** `r pct(pr(c_poor)$share)` of crashes have key conditions missing, mostly minor crashes.

# Conclusion

Victoria's official crash categories describe **how** crashes happen. This project shows that **the situation a crash
happens in decides how likely it is to kill someone**, and that the official categories hide it. Within one category
the death rate varied `r fold`-fold depending on the situation.

The most common crashes, at city intersections, are not the most deadly. **High-speed rural roads and night-time
driving account for `r pct(top2_deaths)` of the `r num(total_deaths)` deaths in the data** from only
`r pct(top2_share)` of crashes. If road-safety effort follows crash counts, it is aimed at the wrong places. If it
follows deaths by situation, it can be aimed where it saves the most lives.

# Reproducing this report {-}

```
Rscript run_all.R        # runs R/01-04 and renders this report (about 3 minutes)
shiny::runApp("app")     # interactive map
```
